lesson.title: Build a Better ls CLI in Rust with Clap
lesson.goal: build a command-line tool in Rust with cargo that parses arguments

sources.title: Build a Better ls CLI in Rust with Clap

steps.title: Create project and parse args
steps.instructions: Run `cargo new best_ls`, add clap with the derive feature to Cargo.toml, and define `#[derive(Parser)] struct Cli { path: Option<PathBuf> }` parsed with `Cli::parse()` in main. Verify with `cargo run -- -h` that the help shows the path argument.

targets.caption: Cli struct with an optional PathBuf path

explanations.topic: clap derive feature makes argument parsing easy
Parser derive adds the parse method
Use -- to pass args through cargo run
Generated help: usage, arguments, options

hints: Add clap to [dependencies] in Cargo.toml with features = ["derive"].
Annotate your struct with #[derive(Parser)] and import clap::Parser and std::path::PathBuf.
In main, write let cli = Cli::parse();
Run cargo run -- -h; the -- separates cargo's flags from your program's.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the "derive" feature on clap, so #[derive(Parser)] fails to compile
Not importing clap::Parser, so Cli::parse() isn't found
Running cargo run -h (shows cargo's help) instead of cargo run -- -h
Using PathBuf without use std::path::PathBuf

steps.title: Add version, about, default path
steps.instructions: Add `#[command(version, about, long_about = "best ls command ever")]` to Cli, then `let path = cli.path.unwrap_or(PathBuf::from("."))` and print `path.display()`. Check `cargo run -- --version` and that running with no args prints `.`.

targets.caption: Clap command attribute adding version and about
Run with --version, then with no args

explanations.topic: #[command(version)] auto-generates a --version flag from Cargo.toml
long_about text shows up in --help output
cli.path is an Option, so unwrap_or supplies a default PathBuf
Defaulting to '.' mirrors ls listing the current directory
PathBuf needs .display() to be printed

hints: Put a #[command(...)] attribute right under #[derive(Parser)] on your Cli struct, listing version, about and long_about.
cli.path is an Option<PathBuf>; use .unwrap_or(...) to fall back to a default.
The default should be PathBuf::from("."), and print it with println!("{}", path.display()).
Remember the `--` in `cargo run -- --version` so the flag goes to your program, not cargo.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `use std::path::PathBuf;`, causing an unresolved type error.
Printing the PathBuf directly with {} instead of calling .display() (PathBuf doesn't implement Display).
Running `cargo run --version`, which prints cargo's version instead of your tool's.
Writing long_about without quotes or misspelling it as longabout.
Using #[clap(...)] syntax that doesn't match the clap 4 `command` attribute with the derive feature.

steps.title: Check path existence with colors
steps.instructions: Use `if let Ok(does_exist) = fs::exists(&path)` and, when false, print "Path does not exist" in red via owo-colors (`.red()`), otherwise print "error reading directory". Run `cargo run -- somebadpath` to see the red message.

targets.caption: Red message for a missing path

explanations.topic: Using fs::exists with if let Ok to check a path
owo-colors crate for colored terminal output
cargo build puts the debug executable in target/debug
fs::exists returns Err when existence can't be confirmed or denied

hints: Use `if let Ok(does_exist) = fs::exists(&path)` and branch on the bool inside.
Add owo-colors under [dependencies] in Cargo.toml (or run `cargo add owo-colors`), then `use owo_colors::OwoColorize;`.
Colorize a string with `"Path does not exist".red()` and print it with `println!("{}", ...)`.
Handle the Err case with an else branch that prints "error reading directory", then run `cargo run -- somebadpath`.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `use owo_colors::OwoColorize;`, so `.red()` is not found.
Writing `owo_colors` in Cargo.toml instead of the crate name `owo-colors`.
Leaving out `--` in `cargo run -- somebadpath`, so the argument goes to cargo instead of your program.
Passing `path` by value to fs::exists and moving it, which breaks later uses. Pass `&path`.
Not handling the Err case from fs::exists (the 'error reading directory' branch).

steps.title: List directory files
steps.instructions: Write `fn get_files(path: &Path) -> Vec<String>` that iterates `fs::read_dir(path)` entries and pushes `file.file_name().into_string().unwrap_or("unknown name".into())`. Loop over `get_files(&path)` in main and print each name.

targets.caption: Helper returning the directory's file names
cargo run lists the current directory

explanations.topic: Returning a Vec<String> as a simple first version of get_files
Using if let Ok to handle fs::read_dir's Result
Iterating directory entries and unwrapping each entry with if let
Converting OsString file names with into_string and unwrap_or
No path argument defaults to the working directory

hints: Write a separate function that takes &Path and returns Vec<String>. Start with an empty vector and return it at the end.
Use `if let Ok(read_dir) = fs::read_dir(path)` and then `for entry in read_dir`. Each entry is itself a Result, so unwrap it with another `if let Ok(file) = entry`.
file.file_name() returns an OsString. Call `.into_string().unwrap_or("unknown name".into())` to get a String you can push.
In main, inside the branch where the path exists, write `for file in get_files(&path) { println!("{}", file); }`. Then run `cargo run` with no arguments.
common_mistakes: Passing `path` instead of `&path` to get_files, which causes a type mismatch or a moved-value error.
Forgetting to import std::fs or std::path::Path.
Treating each directory entry as a DirEntry directly instead of unwrapping its Result first.
Expecting into_string() to return an Option. It returns Result<String, OsString>, but unwrap_or still works.
Not declaring the vector as `let mut`, which gives a borrow error when calling push.
Putting the for loop in the 'does not exist' branch instead of the 'exists' branch.

steps.title: Extract file metadata into struct
steps.instructions: Define `struct FileEntry { name, e_type: EntryType, len_bytes: u64, modified: String }` and `#[derive(strum::Display)] enum EntryType { File, Dir }`, filling them from `fs::metadata(&file.path())` in a `map_data` function. Print the entries with `{:#?}` to verify sizes and types.

targets.caption: Debug output with sizes and types

explanations.topic: Designing a struct to hold file metadata (name, size, modified)
Why the field is e_type: `type` is a reserved keyword
Using an enum to model File vs Dir
strum's Display derive turns enum variants into strings
fs::metadata returns a Result, so match Ok with if let
Bug: passing the directory path instead of file.path()

hints: Define the struct and enum first, then change the Vec you collect into to Vec<FileEntry>.
fs::metadata(...) returns a Result, so use `if let Ok(meta) = fs::metadata(&file.path())`, not `Some`.
Use meta.is_dir() to choose EntryType::Dir or EntryType::File, and meta.len() for len_bytes.
To print with {:#?}, add #[derive(Debug)] to both FileEntry and EntryType. For Display, add strum (with the derive feature) to Cargo.toml and `use strum::Display;`.
common_mistakes: Calling fs::metadata on the directory path instead of file.path(). Every entry then shows the same size and type.
Naming a field `type`, which is a reserved keyword in Rust.
Matching `Some(meta)` against metadata's Result instead of `Ok(meta)`.
Forgetting #[derive(Debug)], so {:#?} fails to compile.
Adding strum without the `derive` feature, so #[derive(Display)] is not found.

steps.title: Render a colored table
steps.instructions: Derive `Tabled` on FileEntry, build `Table::new(get_files(&path))`, apply `.with(Style::rounded())` and color columns/first row via `table.modify(Columns::first(), Color::FG_BRIGHT_CYAN)` etc. Rename headers with `#[tabled(rename = "Type")]` and `#[tabled(rename = "Size B")]`, then run to see the styled table.

explanations.topic: What the tabled crate does: render structs as ASCII tables
Table styles via table.with(Style::...)
Coloring columns and rows with table.modify
Renaming headers with #[tabled(rename)]

hints: Add the tabled crate (cargo add tabled) and derive Tabled on FileEntry.
Replace the print loop with let mut table = Table::new(get_files(&path)); then println!("{}", table).
Style it with table.with(Style::rounded()) and color with table.modify(Columns::first(), Color::FG_BRIGHT_CYAN); use Rows::first() for the header.
Rename headers with #[tabled(rename = "Type")] and #[tabled(rename = "Size B")] above the fields.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to derive Tabled on the enum used as a field (it must implement Display).
Not declaring table as mut before calling with/modify.
Importing Style, Color, Columns or Rows from the wrong module path (they live under tabled::settings).
Using a 0-based column index without realizing Columns::one(1) is the second column.
Misspelling the rename attribute, e.g. #[tabled(name = ...)] instead of rename.

steps.title: Format modified dates with chrono
steps.instructions: Add chrono and set modified using `if let Ok(modi) = meta.modified() { let date: DateTime<Utc> = modi.into(); format!("{}", date.format("%a %b %e %Y")) } else { String::default() }`. Run `cargo run -- src` to see dates in the table.

explanations.topic: Why chrono: modified() returns Result<SystemTime>
Converting SystemTime into DateTime<Utc> with into()
strftime format specifiers for date output

hints: Add chrono to Cargo.toml (e.g. `cargo add chrono`).
meta.modified() returns a Result<SystemTime>; use `if let Ok(...)` with an `else` returning String::default().
Annotate the type: `let date: DateTime<Utc> = modi.into();`, then `date.format("%a %b %e %Y")`.
Don't forget `use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};` at the top of main.rs.
common_mistakes: Naming the binding `mod`, a reserved keyword (use `modi`).
Forgetting the chrono dependency or the `use chrono::{DateTime, Utc}` import.
Omitting the type annotation so `.into()` can't infer DateTime<Utc>.
Missing the else branch, so the if-let doesn't produce a String in both cases.

steps.title: Add JSON output flag
steps.instructions: Add `#[arg(short, long)] json: bool` to Cli, derive `serde::Serialize` on FileEntry and EntryType, and if `cli.json` print `serde_json::to_string(&get_files(&path)).unwrap_or("cannot parse json".to_string())`, else call `print_table`. Verify with `cargo run -- -j` and `cargo run -- --json`.

explanations.topic: #[arg(short, long)] creates both -j and --json from the field name
Extracting the table printing into a print_table function
Adding serde (derive feature) and serde_json to serialize data to JSON
Every nested type (the EntryType enum) must also derive Serialize
unwrap_or supplies a fallback string if serialization fails

hints: Add a `json: bool` field to your Cli struct and annotate it with `#[arg(short, long)]` so clap generates -j and --json.
Add the crates: `cargo add serde --features derive` and `cargo add serde_json`, then add `Serialize` to the derive list of FileEntry and EntryType.
In main, write `if cli.json { ... } else { print_table(path); }` and move the existing table code into a print_table function.
Inside the JSON branch: `println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&get_files(&path)).unwrap_or("cannot parse json".to_string()));` then run `cargo run -- -j`.
common_mistakes: Declaring `json: bool` without `#[arg(short, long)]`, so clap treats it as a positional argument and no -j/--json flag appears in --help.
Deriving Serialize on FileEntry but not on the EntryType enum, causing a 'the trait Serialize is not implemented' error.
Adding serde without the `derive` feature, so `#[derive(Serialize)]` cannot be found.
Forgetting `use serde::Serialize;` at the top of main.rs.
Running `cargo run --json` instead of `cargo run -- --json`, so cargo itself rejects the flag.
